hiragana.title: The Vowels
hiragana.description: Hiragana is the primary phonetic script used in Japanese. It consists of 46 basic characters, each representing one syllable. Start your journey by mastering the vowels.

hiragana.title: The K-Row
hiragana.description: The k-row pairs the consonant "k" with each vowel sound. These characters appear constantly in everyday words, so they are worth memorizing early.

hiragana.title: The S-Row
hiragana.description: The s-row introduces the "shi" sound, which is the first character in this set that doesn't follow the simple consonant-plus-vowel pattern exactly.

hiragana.title: The T-Row
hiragana.description: The t-row has two irregular readings, "chi" and "tsu", instead of "ti" and "tu". Pay close attention to these two.

hiragana.title: The N-Row
hiragana.description: The n-row is fully regular — every character is just "n" plus its vowel. A good confidence-builder after the irregular t-row.

hiragana.title: The H-Row
hiragana.description: The h-row has one irregular reading, "fu" instead of "hu". This row also becomes the base for several sound changes later on.

hiragana.title: The M-Row
hiragana.description: The m-row is fully regular, combining "m" with each vowel sound. You'll see these characters in many common nouns.

hiragana.title: The Y-Row
hiragana.description: The y-row only has three sounds — ya, yu, and yo — because "yi" and "ye" aren't used. These three also combine with other characters later to form contracted sounds.

hiragana.title: The R-Row
hiragana.description: The Japanese "r" sound is a soft blend between an English "r", "l", and "d". Listening to native audio helps a lot with this row.

hiragana.title: The W-Row and ん
hiragana.description: The final set: わ (wa), を (wo, used almost only as the object particle), and ん (n), the only character that's a consonant on its own. This completes the basic 46 hiragana.

katakana.title: The Vowels
katakana.description: Katakana represents the same 46 sounds as hiragana, but is used mainly for foreign loanwords, names, and emphasis. Its characters are more angular.

katakana.title: The K-Row
katakana.description: Just like in hiragana, the katakana k-row combines "k" with each vowel. Many loanwords starting with these sounds come from English.

katakana.title: The S-Row
katakana.description: The katakana s-row follows the same "shi" irregularity as hiragana. You'll see this row often in loanwords for clothing and food.

katakana.title: The T-Row
katakana.description: The katakana t-row keeps the same "chi" and "tsu" irregularities. Many everyday food and electronics words use this row.

katakana.title: The N-Row
katakana.description: The katakana n-row is fully regular, just like in hiragana — "n" plus each vowel.

katakana.title: The H-Row
katakana.description: The katakana h-row again has the "fu" irregularity. This row shows up constantly in food and hospitality loanwords.

katakana.title: The M-Row
katakana.description: The katakana m-row is fully regular. Restaurant menus are full of these characters.

katakana.title: The Y-Row
katakana.description: Just three sounds again — ya, yu, yo — and they often combine with small versions of other characters to make contracted sounds like "tya" or "fya".

katakana.title: The R-Row
katakana.description: The same soft Japanese "r" sound as hiragana, just in its angular katakana form.

katakana.title: The W-Row and ン
katakana.description: ワ (wa), ヲ (wo, rarely used in katakana), and ン (n) complete the basic 46 katakana characters — the same set of sounds as hiragana, in a different script.

katakana.title: Long Vowels and Double Consonants
katakana.description: Katakana uses a long dash (ー) to stretch a vowel sound, and a small ッ to double the next consonant. Both are extremely common in loanwords.

katakana.title: Names and Countries
katakana.description: Foreign names and country names are almost always written in katakana. This is one of the most practical everyday uses of the script.

grammar.title: The Topic Particle は
grammar.description: は (pronounced "wa" when used as a particle) marks the topic of a sentence — the thing being talked about.

grammar.title: The Subject Particle が
grammar.description: が marks the grammatical subject and is often used to introduce new information or emphasize exactly who or what is doing something.

grammar.title: The Object Particle を
grammar.description: を marks the direct object of a verb — the thing that receives the action, such as what is being eaten, read, or watched.

grammar.title: The Location Particle で
grammar.description: で marks the place where an action happens, such as studying at a library or eating at a restaurant.

vocabulary.word: としょかんでべんきょうします

grammar.title: The Question Particle か
grammar.description: Adding か to the end of a sentence turns it into a yes-or-no question, without changing any word order.

grammar.title: The ます Form (Polite Verbs)
grammar.description: Verbs ending in ます are the polite, everyday form used in most conversations — the safest form for beginners to start with.

grammar.title: The て Form (Connecting Actions)
grammar.description: The て form links actions together, makes requests, and is one of the most useful verb forms to learn early.

grammar.title: い-Adjectives
grammar.description: Adjectives ending in い (i-adjectives) can directly precede a noun or end a sentence on their own, without needing a separate "to be" verb.
